name: Pulmonary trunk and arteries
func: The short trunk and its two branches that carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. There the blood drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. They're the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood after birth.

levels.kid:
Most arteries carry bright red blood full of oxygen. But there's one special set that's different!

The **pulmonary trunk** is a big tube coming out of the right side of your heart. It carries tired, used-up blood that has already given away its oxygen. After a short trip, the trunk splits into two branches, one going to your left lung and one to your right lung, like a letter Y.

In your lungs, the blood dumps out the stale air you breathe out and grabs fresh oxygen from the air you breathe in. Then it goes back to the heart, ready for another trip around your body.
levels.hs:
The **pulmonary trunk** leaves the **right ventricle** through the **pulmonary valve**. It is about 5 cm long and 3 cm wide and lies inside the pericardium, at the front of the heart, to the left of the ascending aorta, which it spirals around.

Under the aortic arch, at about the level of the **T4–T5** vertebrae (the sternal angle), it divides into the **right and left pulmonary arteries**. The **right pulmonary artery** is longer and runs horizontally behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava to reach the right lung. The **left pulmonary artery** is shorter and arches over the **left main bronchus**.

Each artery enters the lung at its **hilum** and branches alongside the airways, ending in capillaries wrapped around the tiny air sacs (**alveoli**). Gas exchange happens there.

These arteries carry **oxygen-poor (deoxygenated)** blood, the reverse of most arteries. That's because "artery" means a vessel carrying blood **away from the heart**, regardless of its oxygen content. Pressure in this circuit is low, about 25/10 mmHg, compared with about 120/80 in the aorta.
levels.college:
The pulmonary arteries branch with the **bronchial tree**: lobar, segmental and subsegmental arteries follow their matching bronchi into each **bronchopulmonary segment**, while pulmonary veins run between segments. This lets surgeons remove a single segment.

Relations at the hilum: on the **left**, the pulmonary artery is the **highest** structure; on the **right**, the main bronchus (eparterial bronchus) sits above it. The **ligamentum arteriosum** joins the left pulmonary artery (near its origin) to the aortic arch.

The lungs have a **dual blood supply**: pulmonary arteries for gas exchange and **bronchial arteries** (from the aorta) nourishing the airway walls.

Physiology: the pulmonary circulation is a **low-pressure, low-resistance, high-compliance** system that receives the entire cardiac output. When output rises in exercise, resistance actually **falls**, by **recruiting** unused capillaries and **distending** open ones.

Uniquely, pulmonary arteries **constrict in response to low oxygen** (**hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction**), the opposite of systemic arteries. This diverts blood away from poorly ventilated areas to keep ventilation and perfusion matched. In the upright lung, gravity creates **West zones**: the apex gets less flow than the base.
levels.phd:
**Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV)** is intrinsic to pulmonary artery smooth muscle. The leading model involves **mitochondria as oxygen sensors**: hypoxia alters electron transport and reactive oxygen species signaling, which inhibits **voltage-gated potassium channels (Kv1.5, Kv2.1)**, depolarizes the cell, opens L-type calcium channels and triggers contraction, with additional store-operated calcium entry and Rho-kinase sensitization. Globally, HPV is harmful: at high altitude or in chronic lung disease, generalized hypoxia constricts the whole bed, raising pressure.

**Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)** is a proliferative vasculopathy: endothelial dysfunction, smooth muscle hyperplasia, and **plexiform lesions**. Three signaling imbalances underpin current therapy: low **nitric oxide/cGMP**, low **prostacyclin**, and high **endothelin-1**. Heritable PAH is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in **BMPR2**, a TGF-β superfamily receptor; reduced BMP signaling tips cells toward proliferation and apoptosis resistance. Newer drugs that trap activin-type ligands (rebalancing this pathway) were the first to target remodeling rather than just vasodilation.

At birth, lung inflation and oxygen drop pulmonary resistance dramatically, reversing flow through the **ductus arteriosus**, which then closes (oxygen and falling prostaglandin E2) to become the ligamentum arteriosum. Failure of this transition causes **persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn**.

The right ventricle's fate determines survival in PAH: adaptive concentric hypertrophy eventually gives way to dilation, ischemia and failure.
levels.expert:
**Pulmonary embolism (PE)** is the big clinical event: a clot, usually from the deep veins of the leg, lodges in the pulmonary arteries. It causes sudden **breathlessness**, pleuritic chest pain, fast heart rate, low oxygen and, if massive, collapse. A large **saddle embolus** straddles the trunk's bifurcation. ECG may show sinus tachycardia or, classically but uncommonly, the **S1Q3T3 pattern**; echo may show RV strain and **McConnell's sign** (RV free wall akinesis with apical sparing). **CT pulmonary angiography** is the standard test; **D-dimer** helps rule PE out in low-risk patients.

Neurosurgical patients are high-risk: immobility after spinal or brain surgery, malignancy, and limb weakness. Yet anticoagulation is dangerous after a fresh brain operation or bleed, so timing is a frequent neurosurgery–medicine debate; an **IVC filter** is sometimes used when anticoagulation is not possible.

**Pulmonary hypertension** shows a **loud P2**, a right ventricular heave, raised jugular venous pressure and edema. It is confirmed by **right heart catheterization** (mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg). Chronic clots can cause **chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)**, treatable by surgical **pulmonary endarterectomy**.

Treatment in general terms: anticoagulation for PE, clot-dissolving therapy or catheter/surgical clot removal for massive PE with shock, and pulmonary vasodilator drug classes for PAH, with lung transplantation for end-stage disease.

keyPoints: Carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
Trunk splits under the aortic arch at about T4–T5
Constricts to low oxygen (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction)
Pulmonary embolism: clot from leg veins; diagnosed by CT pulmonary angiography

test.q: Pulmonary arteries carry blood that is:
test.explain: 'Artery' means away from the heart; these carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

test.q: How do pulmonary arteries respond to low alveolar oxygen?
test.explain: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood to better-ventilated lung.

test.q: A large clot straddling the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk is called a ______ embolus.
test.explain: A saddle embolus can block both pulmonary arteries and cause collapse.

test.q: The best standard imaging test for suspected pulmonary embolism is:
test.explain: CTPA shows filling defects in the contrast-filled pulmonary arteries.

test.q: The fibrous remnant linking the left pulmonary artery to the aortic arch is the ligamentum ______.
test.explain: It's the closed fetal ductus arteriosus.
